entries.question: Nico controls Analia's [Bane Alley Blackguard] enchanted with their [Corrupted Conscience]. Analia casts their own [Lay Claim], targeting Nico's Corrupted Conscience. After it resolves, who controls the Bane Alley Blackguard? Who controls the Corrupted Conscience?
entries.reason: Both answers conclude Analia ends up controlling both the Corrupted Conscience and the Bane Alley Blackguard, and the candidate correctly explains that Lay Claim gains control of the aura and the aura’s continuous “you control enchanted creature” effect then gives Analia control of the creature.
entries.answer:
Analia ends up controlling everything. Once Analia's Lay Claim resolves attached to Corrupted Conscience, Analia controls Corrupted Conscience, and because Corrupted Conscience reads "You control enchanted creature," that control-changing effect now works for its new controller — so Analia also controls Bane Alley Blackguard (which Analia owns anyway). Nico controls nothing here afterward.

Why: an Aura's controller is tracked separately from the controller of the thing it's attached to, and changing control of one doesn't change control of the other ([303.4e]). Lay Claim doesn't change control of Bane Alley Blackguard directly; it only takes Corrupted Conscience ([Lay Claim ruling #0] — gaining control of a permanent doesn't drag along Auras attached to it, and an Aura's "you" refers to its own controller). But Corrupted Conscience's own text is a continuous control effect keyed to "you," i.e., whoever currently controls Corrupted Conscience ([303.4m], [110.2b]); with Analia now that player, the grant of control over Bane Alley Blackguard flows to Analia. Bane Alley Blackguard still has infect from Corrupted Conscience, and it does not become newly "summoning sick" in a way that resets — it simply changes controller, so Analia can't attack with it this turn unless it has haste or has been under Analia's control since their turn began.

Also note Corrupted Conscience remains attached to Bane Alley Blackguard; nothing about the Lay Claim resolution moves it ([303.4j]). Analia is the controller of Lay Claim itself, attached to Corrupted Conscience.

This works the same at a two-player or multiplayer table; the only multiplayer wrinkle in the provided rules is that if a control effect ends and the default controller has left the game, the object is exiled ([800.4c]).

entries.answer_gold: Analia controls both permanents. Out of the two auras, Corrupted Conscience has the earlier timestamp, and would normally be applied first. However, the effects from both auras apply in the same layer, applying the Lay Claim's effect would change how the Corrupted Conscience's effect is applied, and applying the Corrupted Conscience's effect would not change how the Lay Claim's effect is applied, so the Corrupted Conscience's effect is dependent on the Lay Claim's effect. The Lay Claim's effect applies first, giving Analia control of Corrupted Conscience, and then the Corrupted Conscience's effect applies, giving Analia control of Bane Alley Blackguard.

Then in layer 7b, Starfield of Nyx sets base power and toughness each equal to mana value. It keeps its card types and supertypes — it's still a nonbasic land (CR 205.4c; Murmuring Bosk ruling #0), and it loses its {T}: Add {W} or {B} ability and its enters-tapped text.

entries.question: Ainsley controls [Furycalm Snarl], [Humility], [Magus of the Moon], and [Crosis's Catacombs] that entered the battlefield in that order. What are the characteristics of the Furycalm Snarl and Crosis's Catacombs?

Because it operates on text, and Yixlid Jailer's effect doesn't alter text (612.3), Volrath's Shapeshifter reads Mistform Skyreaver's printed text — including Flying — and gets it.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents; it works identically in two-player and multiplayer games. entries.question: Nickolas controls [Dryad Arbor]. Aniya casts [Overwhelming Splendor], enchanting Nickolas. After it resolves, can Nickolas tap the Dryad Arbor for {G}?

Also note that the ability being unusable wouldn't matter for classification anyway: a mana ability stays a mana ability even when it can't produce mana (CR 605.2) — but here it isn't merely unusable, it's removed.

If instead Nickolas taps Dryad Arbor for {G} in response to Overwhelming Splendor (while it's still on the stack), the mana ability resolves immediately without using the stack (CR 605.3b, 405.6c) and he gets his {G} before the Aura ever applies. entries.question: Aya controls a [Skullbriar, the Walking Grave] with 3 +1/+1 counters on it. Nico casts [Duplicant] and has it exile Skullbriar, the Walking Grave. What are Duplicant's power and toughness after the imprint ability resolves?

Duplicant's static ability then gives Duplicant "the power, toughness, and creature types of the last creature card exiled with it." That's a setting effect applied in layer 7b [613.4b], overwriting Duplicant's printed 2/4 with 4/4, and Duplicant's base power and toughness become those values [Duplicant ruling #0]. It also gains Zombie and Elemental and stays a Shapeshifter. Note that Duplicant's ability keeps updating: if the counters on the exiled Skullbriar, the Walking Grave card were somehow changed, Duplicant's power and toughness would change too [Duplicant ruling #3].

One nuance: Duplicant ruling #2 says abilities that add or subtract power/toughness (like Death's Shadow's) don't apply to the exiled card, only characteristic-defining abilities that define a *. That ruling is about abilities, not counters; the counters here are counters on the object itself, which set the card's power and toughness in exile per [122.1a].

Timing assumption: I'm assuming the counters were already on Skullbriar, the Walking Grave when it was exiled. If Skullbriar, the Walking Grave had no counters at the moment of exile, Duplicant would simply be 1/1.

Player count doesn't matter here — nothing in this interaction depends on the number of opponents, so the answer is the same in a two-player game or a multiplayer game.

entries.question: Alijah controls [Badlands] and [Conversion]. Alijah then casts [Magus of the Moon]. After that resolves, what color(s) of mana can Badlands tap for?

entries.question: Adriel controls [Wandering Ones] equipped with [Fleetfeather Sandals]. On Nico's turn, they enchant it with [Tightening Coils]. On Adriel's next turn, they activate Fleetfeather Sandals's equip ability, targeting Wandering Ones. After that resolves, does it have flying?

entries.answer:
Both are blue. Painter's Servant is blue (and no longer colorless), and Dress Down is blue.

Why Painter's Servant is blue: color-changing effects are applied in layer 5, and ability-adding/removing effects are applied in layer 6, which comes *after* layer 5. Only afterward, in layer 6, does Dress Down's "Creatures lose all abilities" strip Painter's Servant's abilities; that removal happens too late to undo the color change already applied (CR 613.6 confirms an effect that has started to apply keeps applying even if its source ability is removed).

- Dress Down's cost is {1}{U}, so it is already blue from its mana cost [202.2, 202.2b]. Dress Down is an Enchantment, not a creature, so its own "Creatures lose all abilities" never touches its own abilities.
- Colorless is not a color [Colorless, 105.1], so "colorless" isn't something Painter's Servant keeps alongside blue.
